paragraphs.text: The great fictional detective Sherlock Holmes was introduced to the reading public in December 1887, as a truth-seeking scientist in a chemistry laboratory of a London hospital, excitedly waving a test tube in his acid-stained fingers. ‘I’ve found it! I’ve found it’, his creator has this fictional detective exclaim, ‘I have found a reagent which is precipitated by haemoglobin and by nothing else.’ It would be 13 years before a real test for ‘the differential diagnosis of human blood’ was used by a German medical researcher. Six months later, that test led to the conviction of a murderer.

Holmes’s creator, British writer Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, was a physician who realized the vital importance for solving crimes of a test that distinguished between the blood of humans and that of other animals. Doyle’s letters, interviews and memoirs reveal how he made Holmes the epitome of an eccentric thinking machine; a detective who insisted on conducting investigations based purely on the scientific approach of observation, deduction, experimentation and conclusion. In 56 short stories and four novellas, Doyle developed his hero into a forerunner of today’s forensic scientists – those scientists whose examination of evidence plays a crucial role in helping police solve crimes.

‘Doyle pointed the way to the future,’ says former University of London chemist John Emsley, who has written a book called Molecules and Murder, published by Britain’s Royal Society of Chemistry. In 2002, the Society named Holmes – not his creator Conan Doyle – as an honorary fellow for the pioneering use of forensics. Emsley notes that Doyle drew attention to advances in forensic science emerging toward the end of the nineteenth century. But these techniques were not in general use, other than for autopsies, and their advocates faced an uphill struggle convincing police of their potential. London’s criminal investigation agency, Scotland Yard, only established its Fingerprint Branch in 1901, two decades after the British journal Nature published evidence that fingerprints provided unique identification.

While the authorities hesitated about the use of forensic science in their work, the public read with great enthusiasm the stories of the fictional detective Holmes because he repeatedly solved cases that had supposedly baffled the police by making use of chemical analysis, microscopic inspection, plaster casts of footprints, mathematical calculation, ballistics, fingerprints, codebreaking, handwriting analysis, gunpowder residues, typography and photographic enlargements. Like all scientists, Holmes published his results and claimed to have produced monographs on topics ranging from the ashes of 140 different tobaccos to tattoo marks and ciphers. Although such references to forensic techniques decreased in the later Holmes stories, they still featured in the books until the final adventure in 1927.

This popularization of the scientific approach to solving crime was vital to the emergence of modern forensics, says Ray Murray, a forensic geologist based in Missoula, Montana, and author of Evidence from the Earth. ‘The scientific method … had been around for some time at that point. But Doyle advertised it, he promoted it, he made it a reality.’ Murray points to evidence that Edmund Locard, a French pioneer of forensic, in which he had encountered many instances of what modern criminologists call the exchange principle. This could be, for example, the hairs left on a jacket by a cat. Or it could be the zinc and copper filings from a trouser cuff by which Holmes identified a man who was part of a coin counterfeiting operation. ‘It’s the basis of all television shows like CSI (Crime Scene Investigation),’ says Murray. Locard gave the exchange principle a solid scientific basis, establishing in Lyon, France, in 1910 one of the earliest laboratories devoted to criminal investigation.

Less speculative is the pioneering role of Sherlock Holmes in the technique of linking a particular typewriter with a text. In the short story ‘A Case of Identity’, published in September 1891, the detective remarks to his friend Dr Watson: ‘It is a curious thing … that a typewriter has really as much individuality as a man’s handwriting.’ This story appeared three years before any document examiner wrote about typewriter identification, according to David Crown, who headed the Questioned Document Laboratory of the Criminal Investigation Agency (CIA) in Washington DC for 15 years.

Who then was the inspiration for this forensic Sherlock Holmes? Early biographies of Doyle give that credit to Joseph Bell, a physician and professor of medicine at Edinburgh University in Scotland, who employed the young author as his out-patient clerk at the Royal Infirmary. This seems simplistic, however. Certainly, Bell was renowned for diagnosing the afflictions of many patients at the infirmary by mere observation. As a kind of entertainment at parties, he often also deduced a person’s occupation and place of residence. Yet Bell was a medical detective, as were two other Edinburgh faculty members whose eccentric behaviour Doyle incorporated into the character of the fictional detective. Holmes was a forensic detective. Holmes was a forensic detective and ranged far beyond medical evidence in his investigations.

The true inspiration for Sherlock Holmes can be detected in this passage from ‘The Blanched Soldier’, in which the detective describes his scientific method: ‘The process … starts upon the supposition that when you have eliminated all which is impossible, then whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth. It may be that several explanations remain, in which case on tries test after test until one or other of them has a convincing amount of support.’ These words might equally well have come from a forensic scientist today. More to the point, they are almost certainly the views of Arthur Conan Doyle, the real model for the forensic Sherlock Holmes.
